culture.reserves-strategiques.title: Strategic oil reserves: a country's life insurance
culture.reserves-strategiques.hook: Hundreds of millions of barrels sleep under the salt of Texas, in French tanks and in Japan. Born from the 1973 shock, these stocks have been used only six times in fifty years. In 2026, they became a weapon against the Hormuz crisis, and even against the price of diesel.
culture.reserves-strategiques.tldr.0: After the 1973 embargo, importing countries created the IEA and committed to holding ==at least 90 days of net imports== in stock [1][6].
culture.reserves-strategiques.tldr.1: These reserves have been used collectively only six times. The biggest operation came in March 2026: ==400 million barrels== in response to the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz [3].
culture.reserves-strategiques.tldr.2: A stock does not replace production: it ==buys time==, is expensive to maintain, and each use leaves the country less protected for the next crisis [11][13].

culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.0: 1973: the day the tap was turned off
Rich countries discover they have no plan if oil stops arriving.

In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil-producing countries declared an embargo against countries supporting Israel. The price of a barrel went from about $2.90 before the embargo to ==$11.65 in January 1974==: it almost quadrupled [2].

For Europe, Japan and the United States, the shock was twofold. Fuel became expensive and, above all, no one knew how long the shortage would last. Each country fended for itself, which pushed prices even higher.

Importing countries drew a lesson: they needed ==their own stocks, and a conductor== to use them together. On 18 November 1974, they signed the agreement creating the International Energy Agency (IEA), whose first task was to secure oil supplies [1].
The United States went further: in 1975, in direct response to the embargo, it created its own Strategic Petroleum Reserve [9].

The idea is simple. A country that imports its oil controls neither the wells, nor the straits, nor the wars. All it can do is give itself time. A strategic reserve is therefore insurance: you pay every year for a disaster you hope never to face.
Before the embargo, a barrel was worth about $2.90. In January 1974, it was worth $11.65 [2]. Economists call this episode the first oil shock.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.1: The 90-day rule, and how the taps are opened
An IEA country must be able to last at least 90 days without importing oil.

The IEA's basic rule fits in one sentence: each member country must hold stocks equal to ==at least 90 days of its net oil imports== [6]. A country that produces some of its own oil imports less, so it has to store less.

The European Union has its own, stricter rule. Since a 2009 directive, each state must hold the larger of two quantities: ==90 days of net imports or 61 days of domestic consumption==. The obligation had to be met by 31 December 2012 at the latest [5].

Not all of these stocks are in government hands. IEA countries hold more than ==1.2 billion barrels of public stocks==, and about 600 million more barrels are kept by oil companies because the law requires them to [3].

In a crisis, the IEA can launch a "collective action". Member countries meet, assess how much oil is missing from the market, then jointly decide on a volume to release [3]. Each government then chooses how to provide its share.

There are two main ways. First, the state sells or lends oil from its own reserves. Second, it ==lowers the minimum stock imposed on companies==, which can then sell what they were holding in reserve. In March 2022, more than two-thirds of the effort came from public stocks, and nearly a third from lower company obligations [4].
Japan used this second lever in 2026: it cut the mandatory stock of its refiners and traders from 70 to 55 days, allowing them to put that oil back on the market [13].
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.2: In France: tanks paid for at the pump
A fraction of a cent per litre, for several months of insurance.
In France, the law requires oil operators to keep strategic stocks at all times. The volume is set at ==29.5% of the quantities sold the previous year==, or about 108 days of sales [7].

Two bodies handle it. The Professional Committee for Strategic Petroleum Stocks (CPSSP), tasked since a 1992 law with financing the system, and SAGESS, a company set up at the initiative of oil firms, which buys, sells and stores on behalf of the CPSSP [6].

In total, France keeps ==about 16 million tonnes of hydrocarbons==, two-thirds of which are held by SAGESS [6]. Before MPs in April 2026, its CEO put the country's actual level at between 100 and 110 days [7].

Who pays? You do, a little, every time you fill up. The costs are borne by fuel distributors, without going through the state budget, and managing the stocks costs ==about 0.75 cents per litre== [7]. A drop in the final price, but over billions of litres, it pays for millions of tonnes in reserve.

These stocks were bought over the years, sometimes long ago. According to the Prime Minister's office, the diesel released in October 2026 had been acquired at ==€0.28 per litre==, while the market was then paying €1.10 [6]. That is what makes it possible to sell it at cost while bringing prices down.

Storing crude oil is not enough: in a crisis, you still need refineries to turn it into petrol, diesel or jet fuel. If they are hit, or if the country mostly imports already-refined fuels, crude is of little use.

That is why the European Union requires at least 30 days of stocks, or a third of the obligation, to be held as refined products [5]. In 2022, the public stocks released were mostly crude, while lowering company obligations mostly freed up finished products [4].
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.3: Elsewhere: salt domes, Japanese records and Chinese secrecy
Each country stores in its own way, depending on its geology, its dependence and its secrets.

The American reserve is the best known. The oil sits in ==caverns carved out of salt== at four sites on the Gulf Coast: Bryan Mound and Big Hill in Texas, West Hackberry and Bayou Choctaw in Louisiana. Its capacity is about 713.5 million barrels, and it can deliver up to 4.4 million barrels a day for 90 days before the rate starts to fall [9].

This reserve has been used a lot in recent years. In spring 2022, Washington announced a sale of 180 million barrels, the largest in its history; in October, the stock fell to 405 million barrels, its lowest level since 1984 [10]. In 2026, a new agreement provides for 172 million barrels to be released: in early October, only ==283 million barrels== remained, the lowest level since October 1982 [11].

Japan, which imports almost all its oil, chose to be the best protected. At the end of 2025, it held ==254 days of consumption==, or 470 million barrels: 146 days in state stocks, 101 days with private companies and 7 days in joint stocks with producing countries [13].
In March 2026, Tokyo announced its largest-ever release: 45 days of consumption, nearly 20% of its reserves. The previous record, 25 days, dated from the 2011 earthquake and tsunami [13].

China does not publish its figures. The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates its stocks reached ==nearly 1.4 billion barrels== at the end of 2025, counting the commercial stocks that state companies must keep for emergencies. The share held directly by the state is thought to be about 360 million barrels [14].

Beijing built up this oil very quickly: about 1.1 million barrels a day on average in 2025, according to the same estimate [14]. But without official figures, it is hard to know when and how China draws on its reserves.
Salt domes form watertight caverns, dug by dissolving the salt with fresh water, which can be enlarged if needed [9]. It is far cheaper than building steel tanks for hundreds of millions of barrels.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.4: "For the first time", the stocks are being used to protect purchasing power. Roland Lescure, French Economy Minister, October 2026 [7].

IEA collective actions are rare. Before 2026, there had been only five: the Gulf War in 1991, Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the war in Libya in 2011, and twice in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine [3].

In 2022, IEA countries first decided, on 1 March, to release 60 million barrels; in the end they made nearly 62.7 million available. On 1 April, they added 120 million. In total, ==182.7 million barrels==, about three-quarters of which came from public stocks [4].

Then came 2026. With the war in the Middle East, exports of crude and fuels through the Strait of Hormuz fell to ==less than 10% of their pre-conflict level==. On 11 March, the 32 IEA countries unanimously decided to put 400 million barrels on the market, more than twice the 2022 total [3].

That was not enough to ease the diesel shortage. On 2 October 2026, the G7 agreed to release another 100 million barrels of diesel and crude over four months, with ==a large share of diesel in the first 20 days== [15].

France is doing its part. The government is releasing 10 million barrels of diesel, about one-fifth of the diesel SAGESS held at the end of 2024 [7]. They are sold at cost to distributors, split according to their 2025 market shares, from 28 October, in an operation lasting three months, from November to January [8].

This is a change in nature. These stocks were meant to prevent a physical shortage. In 2026, they are also being used, ==for the first time in France, to lower the price paid at the pump==, as the Economy Minister pointed out [7].
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.5: Does it really bring prices down?
A stock buys time. It does not reopen a strait.

The effects are real but modest. After the big US sale of 2022, the US Treasury estimated it had lowered petrol prices ==by 13 to 31 cents per gallon== (about 3.8 litres), while acknowledging that it is not known exactly how much of the fall in crude prices reached the pump [12].

The market reacts mostly to announcements. After the G7 decision of 2 October 2026, Brent fell 1.48% to $100.8 a barrel [15]. A real drop, but a small one compared with the surge caused by the Hormuz crisis.

In France, the government hopes for a drop of ==12 to 18 cents per litre of diesel==, or about ten euros saved per fill-up on average. The head of TotalEnergies expects more like 8 to 12 cents in his network [8].

The limit is physical: a stock is finite. In Japan, one analyst sums it up: these reserves stabilise prices in the short term, but they ==mainly buy time== and cannot offset a long disruption at Hormuz [13].

Each release also weakens the next line of defence. In the United States, the reserve is at its lowest since 1982 [11]. If a new crisis broke out tomorrow, there would be fewer barrels left to respond.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.6: The debates: cost, political use, transition
Insurance you pay for every year, and hesitate to use.

First debate: cost. Storing millions of tonnes ties up money, tanks and caverns, for oil that is almost never used. In France, the bill goes through the pump price [7]; in the United States, the reserve belongs to the federal government [9]. Its supporters reply that this is the price of insurance.

Second debate: what should these stocks be used for? For some, only real supply disruptions. For others, they can also cushion a price spike. France's use in October 2026, presented as a purchasing-power measure, revived this question [7]. The head of SAGESS had pointed out in April that these were "not sales" but loans to be returned; the government says a sale remains legally possible [6].

Third debate: refilling. An emptied stock must be bought back, ideally when prices are low. In the United States, the administration now offers to ==lend oil to companies==, 40 million barrels in its latest offer, rather than sell it [11]. Japan, for its part, must rebuild reserves it drew down heavily in 2026 [13].

Fourth debate: the energy transition. If countries consume less oil, their imports fall, and the 90-day rule mechanically requires smaller stocks. But as long as lorries, planes and tractors run on diesel and jet fuel, dependence remains high, especially for refined products.

Finally, oil is no longer the only energy stored as a precaution. Gas is also stored before winter, under other rules. For you, the lesson is concrete: when a crisis breaks out far away, part of what happens at the petrol station depends on tanks and caverns you will never see.
culture.reserves-strategiques.didYouKnow: France's 2026 stock release is not only for motorists: it also covers off-road diesel used by farmers and construction firms, as well as heating oil, and more than 300 rural petrol stations are receiving support [8].

culture.barrage-renaissance.title: The Renaissance Dam: the water war on the Nile
culture.barrage-renaissance.hook: Ethiopia has built Africa's largest hydroelectric dam on the Blue Nile. For Addis Ababa, it means light and restored pride. For Cairo, an "existential threat". In between, Sudan hesitates. How a concrete wall became one of the continent's great standoffs.
culture.barrage-renaissance.tldr.0: Egypt relies on the Nile for ==97% of its water==, and more than 80% of that water rises in the Ethiopian highlands [1][2].
culture.barrage-renaissance.tldr.1: The 1929 and 1959 treaties split the river between Egypt and Sudan ==with nothing set aside for Ethiopia==, which does not consider itself bound by them [2].
culture.barrage-renaissance.tldr.2: Inaugurated on 9 September 2025, the dam can store ==74 billion m³== and produce 5,150 MW, in a country where fewer than one in two people have adequate access to electricity [1][9].
culture.barrage-renaissance.tldr.3: Fifteen years of negotiations have produced ==no binding agreement== on filling and on management during droughts [4][6][7].

culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.0.q: The water that reaches Cairo is, for the most part, rain that fell on Ethiopia.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.0.p: When we think of the Nile, we picture the pyramids and the Egyptian delta. But the river is a regional affair: its basin stretches over about ten countries, from Lake Victoria to the Mediterranean. Ten of them are members of the Nile Basin Initiative, the regional cooperation body [5].

The Nile actually has two main branches. The White Nile comes from the Great Lakes region, in the heart of East Africa. The Blue Nile comes down from the Ethiopian highlands. It is swollen by very heavy summer rains.
The two branches meet in Khartoum, Sudan's capital. From there on, there is only one Nile, which crosses the desert all the way to Egypt.

The key point is volume. The Ethiopian highlands supply ==more than 80% of the water that flows into the Nile== [2]. In other words, Egypt, at the very bottom of the river, mostly receives water born in Ethiopia, at the very top.

That is the whole tension of the issue. An upstream country that "owns" the source, and a downstream country that depends on it almost entirely. Specialists call this an upstream-downstream asymmetry. You find it on many large shared rivers, but rarely this starkly.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.1.q: For Cairo, the Nile is not one resource among others: it is almost the only one.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.1.p: Egypt is a country with almost no rain. Its population lives overwhelmingly along the river and in its delta. It relies on the Nile for ==97% of its water== [1].

President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has called the Ethiopian dam an =="existential threat"== to his country's water security [1]. Cairo fears that during a drought, Ethiopia would hold water back in its reservoir instead of letting it through [1].

To understand Egypt's position, you have to go back in history. In 1929, Egypt signed an agreement with Britain, which was then acting on behalf of its East African colonies and Sudan. Egypt obtained ==48 billion m³ of water a year==, Sudan 4 billion, out of an estimated average flow of 84 billion. The text also gave it a veto over major works upstream [2].

In 1959, Egypt and a newly independent Sudan signed a new agreement. The shares rose to ==55.5 billion m³ for Egypt and 18.5 billion for Sudan== [2]. The two countries thus split almost the entire average flow of the river between them.

The problem: these texts provide ==nothing for the other basin countries==, not even for Ethiopia, where most of the water comes from [2]. For Egypt, these agreements establish "historic rights" that must be respected. For upstream countries, they are colonial or bilateral texts they never signed, and which therefore do not bind them [2].

Faced with these treaties, the basin countries tried to build a common framework. The Nile Basin Initiative now brings together ten countries: Burundi, DR Congo, Egypt, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Sudan, South Sudan and Tanzania. Eritrea is an observer [5].

These talks produced a Cooperative Framework Agreement, often called the "Entebbe agreement", after the Ugandan city that hosts the Initiative's secretariat [5]. For upstream countries, it should replace the shares fixed long ago with a sharing arrangement designed for the whole basin.

Egypt and Sudan have not ratified it. Even so, the framework agreement ==entered into force on 13 October 2024==, after ratification by Burundi, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda, followed by South Sudan's accession [5].

It creates a ==Nile River Basin Commission==, presented as the first joint body to manage the river [5]. But a commission without the two downstream countries, which use most of the water, has limited reach. The Nile is left with two opposing legal logics: that of the 1929 and 1959 treaties, and that of the framework agreement.
It is in this context, just as the old order was being challenged, that Ethiopia launched its great project.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.1.b: A veto signed in London and Cairo
The 1929 agreement was concluded between Egypt and Britain. London signed for Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika (today's Tanzania) and Sudan [2].

It granted Egypt ==a veto over construction projects== on the Nile and its tributaries. The upstream countries, once independent, replied that they were not parties to this text and that it does not bind them [2].
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.2.t: The GERD, a nation's building site
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.2.q: "A great achievement not only for Ethiopia, but for all black people." Abiy Ahmed, at the inauguration [1].
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.2.p: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, often called the GERD, is built on the Blue Nile, in western Ethiopia, not far from the Sudanese border. Construction began in 2011 [3].

Its dimensions are extraordinary. The reservoir can hold ==74 billion m³ of water==, almost as much as the Nile's average annual flow estimated at the time of the treaties, 84 billion m³ [1][2]. Planned capacity reaches ==5,150 megawatts== [1]. It is Africa's largest dam by power capacity, though it is not among the world's top ten [1].
AFP puts the cost at ==around $4 billion==, with figures varying by source [1]. For a low-income country, that is a huge sum.

Financing is central to the Ethiopian narrative: the country paid for its dam with its own resources. According to project figures reported by the Ethiopian press, ==91% of the funding==, about 223 billion birr, came from loans by the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia, a state-owned bank [11].

The remaining 9%, about 23.8 billion birr, came directly from the population, through ==bonds and donations== [11]. Ethiopians thus lent or gave money for "their" dam. That is what turned it into a national symbol, far beyond electricity.

Filling took place in stages, during the rainy season, without agreement with the neighbours. In July 2020, Ethiopia said it had reached a first target of ==4.9 billion m³==. In 2021, it aimed for 13.5 billion more [12]. The dam was officially inaugurated on ==9 September 2025== [1].
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.2.b: Filling a reservoir means holding back the river
To generate electricity, a dam needs enough water height in front of its turbines. So it first has to ==hold back part of the flow== over several rainy seasons.

The GERD has 13 turbines. The second filling target, in 2021, was meant to run the first two [12]. The faster the filling, the sooner the electricity arrives, but the less water flows downstream in those years. Hence the importance of the pace, at the heart of the negotiations.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.3.q: For Addis Ababa, the dam does not take water away: it runs it through turbines.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.3.p: A large part of Ethiopia's population still lives without reliable electricity. According to a preliminary World Bank survey, only ==44% of Ethiopians== had at least basic access to electricity in 2025 [9].
That leaves ==nearly 71 million people== without adequate access, mostly in rural areas and around cities [9].

Ethiopia's argument fits in one sentence: a hydroelectric dam does not "consume" water, it uses it to spin turbines, then returns it to the river. Once the reservoir is full, the water keeps flowing to Sudan and Egypt. For Addis Ababa, rejecting the dam would mean condemning the country to stay in the dark to protect agreements it never signed.
The dam also has a regional economic dimension. Ethiopia already sells its electricity to its neighbours. In the 2024-2025 fiscal year, these exports brought in ==more than $118 million== [10].

Kenya is by far the largest customer, with $86.3 million, ahead of Djibouti ($30.9 million) and Sudan ($0.9 million) [10]. For a country short of foreign currency, this revenue matters. And electricity becomes a tool of influence: the more the neighbours buy, the more they have a stake in the dam's stability.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.4.q: Sudan has a lot to gain from the dam, on one condition: knowing what is happening upstream.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.4.p: Sudan is squeezed between the two giants. It is downstream of Ethiopia but upstream of Egypt, with which it shares the 1959 agreement. Its position has often shifted.

The dam can help it. Sudan's irrigation minister acknowledged its benefits: ==electricity, fewer floods, less silt== and better management of Sudan's Roseires dam, a little further down the Blue Nile [14].

But he set a condition: ==a legally binding agreement and an exchange of information== [14]. Sudan wants to know in advance the filling and release dates, as well as the safety documents, to run Roseires safely [14]. A reservoir this large, this close to its border, is also a safety issue for the people downstream.

In September and October 2025, just after the inauguration, floods hit Sudan and Egypt. Cairo accused Ethiopia of causing ==a "man-made flood"== through poorly coordinated water releases. Addis Ababa denied it, called the accusations "false" and blamed the rising White Nile [13].

All this is happening in a country at war. Since 15 April 2023, the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group, have been fighting for power. By January 2024, according to the UN, ==more than 7.3 million people== had been forced to flee their homes [15]. A state at war has fewer means to negotiate, maintain its dams and protect its people from floods.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.5.t: Fifteen years of talks without a deal
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.5.q: Everyone agrees on one principle: do not cause "significant harm". Nobody agrees on what it means.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.5.p: In March 2015, the three countries signed a ==Declaration of Principles== in Khartoum. One of them commits each country to take appropriate measures ==not to cause significant harm== to the others. If harm occurs anyway, the responsible country must discuss with the affected country how to reduce it, and where appropriate, compensation [4].

The text remains general. It sets neither the filling pace, nor rules for managing droughts, nor a mechanism to settle disagreements. These are precisely the points that have been blocking ever since.

The United States then attempted mediation. In February 2020, in Washington, Ethiopia asked to postpone what was meant to be the final round. The US Treasury then met Egypt and Sudan alone, and stated that ==filling should not take place without an agreement== [6].

Talks under the African Union followed, with no result. Egypt and Sudan took the issue to the UN. On 15 September 2021, after more than fourteen months of intermittent negotiations, the Security Council adopted a ==presidential statement==, its first position on the matter [7].

It called for the resumption of African Union-led talks, aiming at a binding agreement [7]. Tunisia had first proposed a resolution, but as Council members could not agree, it fell back on this weaker text [7].

The real sticking point is drought. A study published in 2020 in Nature Communications simulated several situations. During filling, the Aswan reservoir could drop to levels not seen for decades, but the additional risk of shortage for Egypt would remain ==relatively low== [8].

In normal times, once the reservoir is full, the dam would benefit Ethiopia and Sudan without significantly reducing Egypt's water [8]. A ==multi-year drought==, however, would require close coordination between the three countries to limit the damage [8]. That is exactly what Egypt wants written down in black and white, and what Ethiopia refuses to lock in, in the name of its sovereignty.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.t: What the Nile says about water wars
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.q: More than a water war, the Nile is an example of a water peace that cannot get written.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.p: Despite the strong words, the Nile has not seen open war over the dam. The conflict plays out through treaties, statements at the UN, mediations and flow figures. That is often the case: water strains relations more than it starts wars.

The case shows first that ==geography gives power==. The country that controls the source can build without asking permission. But the downstream country has other assets: its diplomatic weight, its alliances, its army, and the long history of its water use.

It also shows that ==international water law remains vague==. Two principles clash: "equitable and reasonable" use, invoked by upstream countries, and the ban on causing "significant harm", put forward by downstream ones. Both appear in the 2015 declaration [4], but no judge is tasked with reconciling them.

Finally, the climate changes the game. Nobody knows when the next long drought will hit the Ethiopian highlands. When it does, the question will no longer be "should there be a dam?" but =="who keeps the water when there isn't enough for everyone?"== [8].
The Renaissance Dam is now built. The debate is no longer about whether it exists, but about the rules for running it. The Nile remains a shared river; it is its management that is not yet shared.

culture.cables-sous-marins.title: Undersea cables: the global internet hangs by a thread
culture.cables-sous-marins.hook: Do you think your messages travel via satellites? In reality, almost all traffic between continents runs along the ocean floor, inside fiber-optic cables. An infrastructure born in the mid-19th century: discreet, fragile, and now a matter of power.
culture.cables-sous-marins.tldr.0: ==About 99% of internet traffic between continents== travels through cables laid on the seabed, not through satellites [1].
culture.cables-sous-marins.tldr.1: The network keeps growing (==1.7 million km in 2025==) and increasingly depends on the tech giants, which already used two-thirds of international capacity in 2020 [2][6].
culture.cables-sous-marins.tldr.2: Anchors, volcanoes, suspected sabotage: ==150 to 200 faults a year==, an ageing repair fleet, and a law of the sea poorly equipped to punish [2][9][15].

culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.0.ti: From tree sap to fiber optics
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.0.qu: Copper wires coated in tree sap: that is how the first global network was born.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.0.pa: The story begins with tree sap. In the mid-19th century, engineers were looking for a way to run an electric wire underwater without the current leaking out. The answer came from ==gutta-percha==, a kind of natural plastic made from the sap of a tree. In 1847, the German Werner von Siemens developed a method to coat wires with it, and in 1850 a first cable linked England and France [4].

The next challenge was the Atlantic. American businessman Cyrus Field founded a company in 1856. In 1858, a cable was laid from Valentia, in Ireland, to Heart's Content, in Newfoundland. Queen Victoria and US President James Buchanan exchanged messages: ==the Queen's took about 17 hours to transmit==. A month later, the cable failed, damaged by excessive voltage [5].

In 1865, the Great Eastern, a giant iron steamship, carried 2,300 nautical miles of cable. The cable snapped mid-ocean and its end was lost. The following year, the new attempt succeeded: it was the ==first lasting transatlantic cable==, and it transmitted 80 times faster than the 1858 one. By the mid-1870s, four more cables had already been laid [5].

Gutta-percha came mostly from territories under British control. As a result, ==the submarine cable industry became almost entirely British== [4]. Owning the cables meant controlling the flow of news, orders and business: a discreet form of power that is still relevant today.

The principle has not changed: a wire laid on the seabed, from one coast to another. But copper has given way to fiber optics, where information travels as light. Today, ==about 99% of internet traffic between continents== goes through these cables [1]. Satellites therefore carry only a tiny share of exchanges: they mainly serve remote areas, ships, planes, or act as a backup when a cable is cut.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.0.bo: The plastic that grew on a tree

Long before plastic, it was gutta-percha, a material taken from the sap of a tree, that protected electric wires in seawater. It made the expansion of the 19th-century global communications network possible, along with British dominance of the industry [4].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.1.ti: How a cable is laid, and repaired
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.1.qu: The network keeps growing, but the number of faults stays stable: 150 to 200 a year [2].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.1.pa: According to the specialist firm TeleGeography, there were ==570 cable systems in service== in early 2025, more than in any other year in two decades, plus 81 more planned [3]. Placed end to end, telecom cables add up to about ==1.7 million kilometers==, compared with 1 million in 2014 [2]. That is more than forty times around the Earth.

A cable does not look like a big pipe. At its core are a few pairs of optical fibers, as thin as hairs, protected by layers of metal and plastic. In the deep sea, where nothing threatens it, it stays thin and light. Near the coast, where anchors and trawlers pass, it is wrapped in steel wires and often buried under the seabed. Along the route, repeaters powered with electricity from the shore regularly boost the light signal.

Laying a cable requires a ==cable ship==: a specialized vessel that carries thousands of kilometers of cable in its tanks and unrolls it slowly along a route studied in advance. When a cable breaks, a ship of the same kind must come and fish it out, sometimes from several kilometers deep, repair it on board, then lay it back down.

The problem: ==these ships are scarce and ageing==. According to TeleGeography, about two-thirds of cable maintenance ships will have reached the end of their service life by 2040. It would take nearly ==3 billion dollars== to build some twenty new ones (15 to replace old ships, 5 more) and avoid repair delays [9].

Making and laying these cables is a job for specialists. It has long been dominated by three companies: America's SubCom, France's Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN) and Japan's NEC [14]. The newcomer is Chinese: HMN Tech, whose predecessor was majority-owned by Huawei, has made its mark by offering lower prices [14].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.1.bo: ASN, a champion taken over by the state
Alcatel Submarine Networks, based in France, says it has installed more than 750,000 km of optical submarine cable worldwide and operates a fleet of seven cable ships [8].
Finnish group Nokia, which owned it, sold 80% of the company to the French state, at an enterprise value of 350 million euros. The sale was completed on 31 December 2024 [8].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.2.ti: Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon: the new masters of the seabed
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.2.qu: In 2020, four companies used two-thirds of all international capacity [6].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.2.pa: For more than a century, cables belonged to telecom companies, often national ones, grouped in consortiums to share the bill. That model still exists. But one player has taken center stage: the tech giants.

According to TeleGeography, in 2020 ==Google, Facebook (now Meta), Amazon and Microsoft used about two-thirds of all international capacity in use worldwide==. Their priority: linking their data centers to each other and to the internet's major exchange points [6].
Their weight varies a lot by route. On the Atlantic, between North America and Europe, they accounted for ==91% of used capacity==, but only 12% between Europe and East Asia [6].

Why build your own cables? Video, cloud services and artificial intelligence keep pushing data volumes up. Rather than renting capacity from operators, these companies prefer to own their "pipes", choose their routes and control their costs. It is the same logic as a factory buying its own fleet of trucks instead of using a carrier.

One example is ==2Africa==, a project in which Meta takes part alongside operators such as Orange, Vodafone, China Mobile International and Telecom Egypt. This cable of about ==45,000 kilometers== circles Africa and links it to the Middle East, Europe and Asia. It reaches 33 countries and 46 landing points, and its construction was declared complete in November 2025 [7].

For Africa, it is a real change: 2Africa is presented as the first cable to directly connect East and West Africa in a single continuous system [7]. More cables in principle mean more competition between providers, lower wholesale prices, and less risk of a total outage when a cable breaks.

This concentration also raises a question. When a few private companies use or own a growing share of the internet's "highways", their weight in dealing with states and operators grows. Some see it as a source of efficiency and investment, others as a risk of dependence.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.3.qu: Like oil, data flows through a handful of straits.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.3.pa: Cables are not spread at random. They follow the shortest path between major economic hubs. So they cluster in a few unavoidable passages, where a canal, a strait or a well-placed coastline draws every route.

The most sensitive is the ==Red Sea==. To go from Europe to Asia, the shortest route crosses the Mediterranean, passes through Egypt, then runs down the Red Sea toward the Bab el-Mandeb strait, off Yemen.

In February 2024, this passage showed how fragile it is. The cargo ship Rubymar, hit by Houthi missiles in mid-February, drifted before sinking. A few days later, ==three cables (Seacom, AAE-1 and EIG)== were cut in the same area. According to US officials, the anchor dragged by the ship is the most likely cause [10].

According to an estimate by Hong Kong operator HGC, these cables carried about ==a quarter of the traffic flowing through the region==. Traffic was rerouted to other cables. But the repair got complicated: insurance and security guarantees were needed to send a ship into a conflict zone [10].

At the other end of the Mediterranean, ==Marseille== has become a major European hub for cables coming from Africa, the Middle East and Asia. The new SeaMeWe-6 cable, for example, links Singapore to France [14].

In Asia, ==Singapore== and the Strait of Malacca play the same role as a node. Further east, the ==Luzon Strait==, between Taiwan and the Philippines, carries many cables between Northeast Asia and the rest of the world. It is both an earthquake zone and at the heart of tensions around Taiwan.

These chokepoints suit operators, who share landing stations and permits. But they create fragility: a single accident can hit several cables at once. That is why new projects look for bypass routes, like 2Africa, which goes around the African continent [7].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.4.qu: Most of the time, the culprit is an anchor or a trawl. The hardest part is proving otherwise.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.4.pa: According to the International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC), which brings together industry players, there are ==150 to 200 faults a year==, a number that stays stable even as the network grows. ==70 to 80% are accidents caused by human activity==, mainly fishing and ship anchors. The rest come from natural hazards or technical failures [2].

Nature can strike hard. On 15 January 2022, the eruption of the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai undersea volcano damaged the cable linking the Tonga archipelago to the rest of the world. For ==five weeks==, the country could communicate only through a handful of satellite links, until the cable was repaired on 22 February [11].

In the Baltic Sea, the string of incidents took on another dimension. According to a count by the AP news agency, ==at least 11 cables were damaged there between October 2023 and January 2025== [12]. The most closely followed case: on 25 December 2024, the Estlink 2 power cable between Finland and Estonia, along with several telecom cables, was damaged. Finland seized the tanker Eagle S, which it links to the "shadow fleet" carrying Russian oil, on suspicion of dragging its anchor along the seabed [12].

Investigations often stumble on the same question: was it deliberate? In several cases, shipowners spoke of an accident, and operators point out that fishing and anchors remain the leading causes of damage in these waters [12].

Around Taiwan, cuts are also recurring. In February 2025, the Taiwan-Penghu No. 3 cable was found severed after the departure of the Hong Tai 58, a Togo-registered ship commanded by a Chinese captain. In June 2025, a Taiwanese court sentenced the captain to ==three years in prison== [13].
The captain blamed rough seas and said he did not know a cable was there. The court noted that the cable was marked on the ship's charts [13].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.4.bo: A ship dragging its anchor can damage a cable without meaning to. To speak of sabotage, intent must be proven: the ship's track and the state of the seabed are not always enough.
That is why the sentence handed down in Taiwan in 2025 was described as a first on the island in an undersea cable case [13].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.5.ti: A US-China battle under the sea
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.5.qu: Who makes, lays and maintains the cables? For states, the question has become strategic.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.5.pa: The data flowing through cables is usually encrypted. But for states, a cable's builder is no detail: it knows the network, supplies the equipment and handles maintenance. Hence fears of access to data, or of a cut-off in a crisis.

The best-known example is ==SeaMeWe-6==, a cable worth about ==600 million dollars== that links Singapore to France via a dozen countries. China's HMN Tech was due to build it: its bid, around 500 million dollars, was about a third cheaper than the initial proposal from America's SubCom [14].

According to a Reuters investigation, the US government, worried about the risk of Chinese spying, ran a campaign of pressure and incentives aimed at consortium members. The contract eventually went to SubCom. In the meantime, the US Commerce Department had added HMN Tech to its sanctions list, accusing it of supplying the Chinese military [14].

Again according to Reuters, this is not an isolated case: Washington reportedly intervened in ==at least six private cable projects in the Asia-Pacific region in four years== [14]. Operators China Mobile and China Telecom, for their part, left the SeaMeWe-6 consortium [14].

For countries caught between the two powers, the choice is tricky. A Chinese cable can cost less, as HMN Tech's bid shows. A cable built by a Western company avoids friction with Washington. Cables have thus become part of the technology rivalry, just like 5G or microchips.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.6.qu: The law of the sea requires punishment, but gives few means to act far from the coast.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.6.pa: Offshore, cables are protected by old law. The 1884 Paris Convention for the Protection of Submarine Telegraph Cables inspired Article 113 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea [15].

This article requires states to make the breaking or injury of a cable an offence. But it does not give them the power to take enforcement measures against foreign ships on the high seas [15]. In other words: a country can see its cable cut far from its shores without being able to stop the suspect ship.

So states are responding in other ways. In January 2025, NATO launched the =="Baltic Sentry"== mission: warships, maritime patrol aircraft and naval drones to watch over the Baltic and deter sabotage [12].

On 21 February 2025, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for foreign policy presented an ==action plan on the security of submarine cables==. It covers telecom and power cables, around four strands: prevention, detection, response and recovery, deterrence. Deterrence includes sanctions against hostile actors and the "shadow fleet" [1].
The other response is economic: multiply routes so that one cut cable does not cut everything, and build new repair ships. A damaged cable stays useless as long as no ship can go and fix it [9].

For you, these cables are invisible, but they are behind every streamed video, every payment to a foreign website, every video call with the other side of the world. In well-connected regions, a cut usually means a slowdown while traffic is rerouted, as in the Red Sea in 2024 [10]. But for an island linked by a single cable, like Tonga in 2022, one cut can stop everything [11].
To watch: the renewal of the repair fleet, the investigations in the Baltic and in Taiwan, and the race between the United States and China to lay tomorrow's cables.

news.2026-10-21-samarkand-asie-centrale-: Samarkand: Washington goes after Central Asia's minerals, where China is already settled in
The US top diplomat brought together five Central Asian countries. On the table: a trade route that bypasses Russia, and critical minerals.
On Monday in Samarkand (Uzbekistan), Marco Rubio opened talks with the foreign ministers of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, before leaving for India [1][2].

The United States and the five countries issued a joint statement backing investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures. The parties also see more opportunities to extract and process minerals [2][3].

Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords (space cooperation), and Marco Rubio met Kazakhstan's foreign minister on trade, energy, critical minerals and technology [1]. Chinese companies have already signed several energy deals, which Washington is trying to counter [1].
The key point: the United States wants its share of Central Asia's minerals, a landlocked region where China and Russia have long carried weight [1][3].

The Trans-Caspian route crosses the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus instead of Russia: that is what makes it attractive to landlocked countries that want to sell elsewhere. For now, the statement is political backing: investment amounts are not given in the sources consulted [2][3].

Critical minerals go into batteries, chips and weapons. The more the big powers compete for them, the more their prices can become unstable, and that eventually shows up in the price of electric cars and electronics.

news.2026-10-21-inde-petrole-russe-droit: Russian oil: Washington pauses its threat of tariffs of up to 100% and sends Rubio to see India's biggest refinery
A US law would allow tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the biggest buyers of Russian oil, including India. It is on hold while a visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar takes place.

The sanctions law would target the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas, including India and China, with tariffs of up to 100% on the goods they sell to the United States. For now it is suspended [1][2].

Marco Rubio, who called India an "important ally", says Donald Trump wants to use a 60-day window to measure the effect of these tariffs. US Ambassador Sergio Gor expects a decision within about ten days [1][2].

The Secretary of State was due in Mumbai on Tuesday, then at the Jamnagar refinery, with energy on the agenda; he is skipping New Delhi, which irritates people in India [2][3]. India's Commerce Minister says the first phase of the trade deal is concluded and in legal drafting [2].

Washington holds a very powerful tool: taxing countries that buy Russian oil. But using it against India, a heavyweight partner, would risk upsetting an ally and making Indian goods more expensive [1][2].

US tariffs on Indian goods were already raised to 50% in 2025 because of Russian oil, then brought down to 18% [2]. Trade between the two countries grew by nearly 12% in 2025, to about $240 billion [3]. The results of Tuesday's talks are not in the sources consulted.
If 100% tariffs hit India or China, products such as generic medicines, textiles or electronics could cost more in the shops. The threat remains suspended: a decision is expected in the coming days.

news.2026-10-21-bangladesh-croissance-fm: Bangladesh: growth could fall to its lowest level in nearly forty years
The IMF expects only 3.2% growth for fiscal year 2026-2027 and inflation close to 11%.

In its October forecasts, published on 13 October at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the IMF expects Bangladesh to grow 3.2% in fiscal year 2026-2027, down from the 4.3% it forecast in April [1][2].
If confirmed, this would be the weakest annual growth since fiscal year 1988-1989 (3.11%) [1].

The IMF also expects average inflation of 10.9%, higher than the World Bank's 8.6%. In September, inflation was 8.34% according to the country's statistics bureau [1]. The World Bank (3.4%) and the Asian Development Bank (4%) have also cut their forecasts [1][2].
The key point: a country that long grew fast now faces weak growth and rising prices at the same time [1].

For an economy that makes clothes for a large part of the world, such a slowdown weighs on wages, jobs and orders [1]. The three big institutions agree on the direction (less growth) but not on the size: that is why these figures should be read as forecasts, not results [1][2].
A large share of the clothes sold in France is sewn in Bangladesh. A country that is slowing down while its costs rise can, over time, shift clothing prices or delivery times.

news.2026-10-21-irak-kirkouk-bp-champs-p: Iraq: BP returns to run Kirkuk's four big oil fields
The fields pass from Iraqi state companies to a joint operating body with BP, which aims for 450,000 barrels a day.

On Thursday 15 October, operation of Kirkuk's four big fields passed from the state companies North Oil and North Gas to a joint operating body with BP. Iraq's oil minister oversaw the handover by video link [1][2].
The aim is to raise output to 450,000 barrels a day. The contract had been activated in October 2025, with starting output of about 328,000 barrels a day [2][3].

In March, BP had pulled out its staff for safety reasons during the regional war, and the state-run North Oil Company had taken over operating the fields [3]. The next phase includes training ministry staff and transferring know-how [2].
The key point: Iraq is bringing a Western giant back onto its oldest fields, at a time when oil sells for a lot [1][2].
The country is a major producer, but its export routes depend on the Strait of Hormuz, now under tension. Producing more in Kirkuk only makes sense if the oil can get out [2].
More Iraqi oil on the market can help calm fuel prices. But as long as the Strait of Hormuz remains fragile, the effect at the pump stays uncertain.

news.2026-10-21-riyad-conference-investi: Riyadh: under Houthi missiles, the investors' showcase goes partly remote
Saudi Arabia is letting executives follow its big investment conference online, after attacks on the capital.

According to sources cited by The Standard, Saudi Arabia is letting executives attend its FII investment conference remotely, after attacks [1]. Oil bosses have pulled out, but the forum is still planned in person [2].

The Houthis hit Riyadh's main airport, and Saudi Arabia intercepted new Houthi missile attacks on the capital [2]. Next month's Misk Global Forum was cancelled, and the 6th edition of the Red Sea film festival is postponed to the 4th quarter of 2027, without its organisers citing the war [2][3].
In its 19 October note, BNP Paribas forecasts for 2026 a 2% fall in GDP for the Middle East and North Africa and 4.8% for the Gulf countries, with only Oman keeping positive growth (4.1%) [4].
The key point: even the country that wants to become the Gulf's economic showcase must now adapt its big events to the war [1][2].

These events are meant to attract foreign capital. Seeing them cut back or cancelled shows that security risk weighs on Saudi Arabia's plans to diversify its economy [2][4]. BNP's figures are a bank's forecast, not a result.
When the Gulf is unstable, oil stays expensive. Brent traded around $108 a barrel on 19 October [4]. That eventually shows up in the price of fuel and plane tickets.

news.2026-10-21-soudan-frappe-drone-fron: Sudan: a drone strike kills more than 150 people near the South Sudan border
Another tragedy in Sudan's war, reported in OkayAfrica's African news roundup of 20 October.
OkayAfrica reports, in its African roundup of 20 October, that a drone strike killed more than 150 people near the border between Sudan and South Sudan [1].
The sources consulted do not allow us, at this stage, to confirm the exact location, who carried out the strike or the final toll: these need checking before anyone repeats them [1].
The key point: the war in Sudan keeps killing civilians by the dozens and hundreds, using drones [1].
The sources consulted give no other details on the economic consequences of this strike: the story will be completed once dedicated sources are available.

This war is far away, but it affects one of the poorest countries in the world and transport routes for African oil. It is a reminder that a country's security can quickly decide what it is able to sell.
dead in the drone strike, toll to be confirmed
news.2026-10-21-ue-sommet-gaz-140-pource: Gas costs 140% more than in February: Europeans bring out emergency measures before winter
At the mid-October summit, EU leaders agreed first energy measures, while the 2028-2034 budget divides them.
Ursula von der Leyen said EU gas prices have risen 140% since February and diesel has doubled. She cited energy vouchers for low-income families in France and Romania [1].

Leaders agreed short-term measures: extending the temporary state-aid framework, postponing certain obligations under the methane regulation by a year, launching a dialogue on refining capacity and strengthening joint energy purchasing [2][3].
Talks on the 2028-2034 EU budget remain tense: the Council wants a deal before the end of 2026 so that money flows without interruption from January 2028 [2][3].
The key point: Europe is heading into winter with much more expensive gas and is responding with short-term measures rather than deep reform [1][2].
State aid lets governments support their companies and households, but it costs public money at a time when the common budget is contested [2][3].
More expensive gas shows up in heating and electricity bills, and in the price of goods that need a lot of energy. States can offset part of it with aid, paid for by taxes.
